scenarios.title: Where You Live
scenarios.text: Half the roster lives in the same glass tower downtown, with a rooftop pool and a doorman who knows everyone's name. The rent is a quarter of your salary.

choices.label: Rent something modest
choices.result: You rent a two-bedroom twenty minutes from the facility, above a bakery. The teammates call it 'the bakery'. You save more in a month than some of them save in a year, and the commute is short.

choices.label: Move into the tower
choices.result: The lease in the tower gets signed on a Tuesday. The pool parties are legendary and the elevators are full of teammates, and the rent comes out of every check like a tax.

choices.label: Room with a teammate
choices.result: Splitting a place with another rookie is cheaper and louder than you planned. You never eat dinner alone, and you learn more about him than you ever wanted to.

scenarios.title: Homesick in {town}
scenarios.text: Nobody in {town} knows your name yet. Practice ends at four, the apartment is very quiet on Tuesday nights, and the only voice you hear after dinner is the television.

choices.label: Call home every night
choices.result: You call home every night for a week. {parent} starts saving up stories for you like he used to before school, and {sibling} grabs the phone at the end to complain about homework.

choices.label: Make the city yours
choices.result: You pick one new neighborhood every Tuesday and walk it until dinner. By October, {town} has a coffee shop that knows your order.

choices.label: Bury it in work
choices.result: Every quiet night ends in the film room. You become the best-prepared rookie on the roster and the loneliest one, and the cleaning crew starts saying goodnight to you.

choices.label: Keep the Sunday call
choices.result: You kept the Sunday call through four years of college, and you keep it now. The first Sunday in {town}, {sibling} answers and talks for an hour.
choices.lock_text: having promised to call home every week

scenarios.title: The Backup Wants Your Job
scenarios.text: {backup} is on the practice squad and has been kicking very well where the coaches can see: long ones after practice, clean ones in team drills, and a few reporters have noticed.

choices.label: Kick with {backup}
choices.result: You ask {backup} to share your warmups. It makes you both better, and it makes the coaches' decision harder, which is fine.

choices.label: Out-work {backup}
choices.result: Every day for a month, you stay later than {backup}. The coaches notice the hours more than the kicks, and {backup} starts leaving earlier, which tells you something.

choices.label: Let the coaches decide
choices.result: The practice squad isn't your problem, you decide. Your kicking stays the same, and so does the whispering, and {backup} stops saying good morning.

scenarios.title: The New Holder Midseason
scenarios.text: {holder} is hurt, and the replacement holder is a backup quarterback who has never held for a kick. The quarterback has soft hands, a nervous laugh and four days before Sunday.

choices.label: Teach the new holder
choices.result: You stay after practice every day with the backup quarterback until the laces spin right. By Friday the holds are clean.

choices.label: Ask for the punter instead
choices.result: The punter has held before, you point out to {coach}. The coach agrees, the punter shrugs, and the relieved quarterback buys you lunch the next day.

choices.label: Visit {holder}
choices.result: You visit {holder} in the training room and bring the new holder along for a lesson. Two holders and a kicker in one cramped room, laughing.

scenarios.title: The Kick Everyone Saw
scenarios.text: A clip of your practice-field trick shot, the ball off the crossbar and into a trash can forty yards away, goes around the league overnight. Your phone has two hundred new messages.

choices.label: Make a few more
choices.result: You film a series with the specialists. It's fun, the club's social media team loves it, and the coaches don't.

choices.label: Let it be one clip
choices.result: A thank-you post, and that's all. The clip fades in a week, the coaches never mention it, and you're a little sorry you didn't enjoy it more.

choices.label: Use it for charity
choices.result: You turn the clip into a charity challenge: a donation for every kid who sends in their own trick shot.

scenarios.title: Contract Year: Prove It
scenarios.text: It's the last year of your rookie deal, and the front office wants to see one more season before it talks.

choices.label: Put your head down
choices.result: You stop reading anything about contracts and kick. Your agent handles the rest, and the season feels lighter for it.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what they want
choices.result: You ask {coach} exactly what the club needs from you this year. The answer is two things, and both are fixable.

choices.label: Push for a deal now
choices.result: You have your agent push for an extension before the season. The club says no, politely, and remembers that you asked.

scenarios.title: The Quarterback's Ego
scenarios.text: The franchise quarterback blames the special teams in a press conference, by name, on camera. Twenty minutes later the reporters are standing at your locker with their phones already recording.

choices.label: Talk only about your job
choices.result: Your job is the only thing you'll talk about, and you say it calmly three times. The quarterback notices, and so does the locker room, in different ways.

choices.label: Fire back
choices.result: Special teams aren't the problem, you say, looking straight into the camera. It's the clip of the week, and the quarterback stops talking to you until December.

choices.label: Talk to him privately
choices.result: You find him at his locker after practice and ask what he actually meant. It turns out he was angry at himself. He says so at the next press conference.

scenarios.title: The Owner's Gala
scenarios.text: Black tie, the owner's charity gala, and a donor who wants a photo and then a favor: a visit to his company's party next week.

choices.label: Take the photo, skip the favor
choices.result: The photo is easy; the favor isn't. You smile, say your schedule is full, and he's disappointed for about a minute and forgets about it by dessert.

choices.label: Do the favor
choices.result: His company party is two hours of handshakes and lukewarm food, and at the end a check for the gala's charity with your name on it.

choices.label: Slip out before the auction
choices.result: An hour in, you slip out before the auction starts. Nobody asks you for anything, you're asleep by ten, and practice the next morning feels easy.

scenarios.title: The Specialists' Dinner
scenarios.text: The kicker, the punter and the snapper have had a dinner every Thursday since camp. A new punter wants in, he's nervous about asking, and the other two are looking at you.

choices.label: Invite the new punter
choices.result: The new punter gets the invitation from you, and four turns out to be louder than three. The dinner gets better, and he stops eating lunch alone in his car.

choices.label: Keep it to three
choices.result: Three is the number, you decide. It stays easy and familiar, and the new punter eats alone on Thursdays for a month. You notice every time.

choices.label: Make it a unit dinner
choices.result: The whole special teams unit comes. It's chaos, two tables pushed together and a waiter who quits halfway, and it's the best night of the season.

scenarios.title: The Trick Play
scenarios.text: The new coordinator wants a fake field goal with you throwing the pass. You haven't thrown a football in a game since high school, and the backup quarterback is already laughing.

choices.label: Practice the throw
choices.result: You throw fifty passes a day for a week until the ball stops wobbling. The coordinator puts it in the playbook.

choices.label: Pitch a different fake
choices.result: A fake where the holder runs and you just block, you suggest. The coordinator likes it better, and {holder} is thrilled to finally get a carry.

choices.label: Say you're just a kicker
choices.result: Kickers kick, you say with a grin. The coordinator doesn't grin back, the fake goes to the punter, and you spend the season watching him get the credit.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Slump
scenarios.text: Your first real slump. The misses come in practice, then in your sleep, and every veteran in the room has a theory about your plant foot that he wants to share at lunch.

choices.label: Listen to one person
choices.result: You pick the one voice you trust, {coach}, and tune out the rest. The fix is small and it takes.

choices.label: Try every theory
choices.result: Every veteran's advice gets tried in one week. Your form is a mess by Friday, your confidence is worse, and at least they all feel listened to.

choices.label: Kick until it comes back
choices.result: Two hundred balls a day, until something clicks. Your leg is sore and heavy, the snapper starts bringing you ice, and on the ninth day the slump breaks.

choices.label: Call someone who helped before
choices.result: The people who helped the last time you struggled pick up on the first ring, and the plan you made with them then still works now.

scenarios.title: The Rookie on a Run
scenarios.text: The streak is a month old. Rookie card companies are calling your agent, a talk show wants you, and the specialists have stopped saying the word 'streak' anywhere near you.

choices.label: Never say the word
choices.result: Not one word about the streak, from you or anyone in the specialists' room. The snapper even unplugs the television when the highlights come on.

choices.label: Enjoy the attention
choices.result: Interviews, a card shoot and a podcast, all in one week. It's fun and a little dizzying, and by Friday practice you're more tired than you've been all year.

choices.label: Credit {holder} and the snapper
choices.result: Every interview turns into a speech about the snapper and {holder}. The specialists' group chat is very happy, and {holder} prints one quote and frames it.

scenarios.title: The Veteran They Signed to Push You
scenarios.text: The club signs a thirty-four-year-old kicker 'for depth'. He has a locker two down from yours, a ring from another club, and everybody in the building knows what 'depth' means for a rookie.

choices.label: Learn from the veteran
choices.result: The veteran watches your warmup once and fixes your hip turn in five minutes. He doesn't make a speech about it, and you wonder why he'd help his competition.

choices.label: Compete every day
choices.result: Every practice becomes a contest you refuse to lose. The veteran is tired by October and you aren't, and {coach} starts calling your name first in meetings.

choices.label: Go out and forget about it
choices.result: You go out with the other rookies every night that week to stop thinking about the veteran. It works until Monday, when {coach} notices you look tired.
